capabilities.name: Identity & access management

The internal function (schedule periodic physical-access control reviews and collect disposal/destruction evidence for audit) is covered by a free, self-hostable OSS compliance-automation tool. comply/OpenComply (Apache-2.0) is a fitting SOC2-focused control and evidence-tracking replacement; Eramba Community is an equally acceptable alternative per the swap guidance. Not inherent — this is software with a clear OSS equivalent, not a cloud substrate, legal service, or physical hardware.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are managed/SaaS because this capability is fundamentally about facilities, hardware, and endpoints rather than application code — there is no meaningful open-source "component" you embed in a software stack to control physical door access or destroy data-center drives. For self-managed endpoints/servers, an open-source disk sanitizer such as nwipe (NIST 800-88 purge) or the built-in `cryptsetup`/`blkdiscard` crypto-erase can supplement the MDM path, but in a greenfield cloud build the provider handles media destruction. Primary control set is: inherit DC controls from the cloud provider, gate your own facilities with cloud access control, enforce encryption+remote-wipe via MDM for crypto-shredding, and track reviews/evidence in a GRC platform.

capabilities.name: Infrastructure, network boundary & endpoint protection
capabilities.description: General controls over technology infrastructure (networks, servers, cloud) supporting reliable processing, boundary defenses (firewalls, segmentation, IDS/IPS) protecting the perimeter, and controls to prevent, detect, and remediate unauthorized or malicious software.

stack.name: OWASP Coraza WAF (+ OWASP Core Rule Set)
stack.why: Coraza engine and the OWASP Core Rule Set are both Apache-2.0 (verified, no relicensing) — a self-hostable Go WAF enforcing application-boundary defense on live customer traffic, fully embeddable in a sold product. Correctly replaces proprietary managed-SaaS Cloudflare, which has no self-hostable OSS core. (Coraza covers only the WAF layer; DDoS and Zero-Trust access were also Cloudflare functions — a functional gap, not a license gap.)

stack.name: Cilium + Hubble (eBPF)
stack.why: Both Apache-2.0 (CNCF-graduated). Kernel-loaded eBPF fragments carry GPL/dual notices but the distributed project license is Apache-2.0, so there is no copyleft distribution exposure. Product-embeddable in any role; keep is correct.

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: CrowdStrike Falcon is a proprietary EDR/XDR product with no free tier or free self-hosting — it only functions on a paid subscription. Its internal compliance function (endpoint/host, network-boundary and workload protection for SOC2) is covered by Wazuh, a free, self-hostable open-source security platform providing endpoint detection/response, log analysis, file-integrity monitoring, and threat detection across endpoints, servers and cloud workloads. Swapped per the paid-EDR -> Wazuh rule.

stack.name: Falco
stack.why: Apache-2.0 (verified, CNCF-graduated) eBPF/syscall runtime IDS observing our own hosts and containers out-of-band. Corrected from keep-exception to keep: keep-exception is reserved for components that would otherwise fail policy and survive only via the carve-out; Falco's Apache-2.0 license is product-embeddable on its own merits and needs no exception. Role is honestly internal-infra, but the license — not the carve-out — is why it is kept.

capabilities.stack_notes: Scoped to a greenfield cloud/Kubernetes stack. Cloudflare handles the perimeter (boundary defense), Cilium handles internal segmentation, and Falcon+Falco cover endpoint/workload anti-malware and runtime intrusion detection. Open-source-only alternative to Falcon: Wazuh (HIDS, anti-malware, file-integrity monitoring). If not on Kubernetes, substitute cloud-provider network firewalls (e.g. AWS Network Firewall) for Cilium.

capabilities.name: Vulnerability management & remediation
capabilities.description: Scheduled scanning of infrastructure and software for known vulnerabilities and configuration drift, with tracked, risk-prioritized remediation to resolution within defined SLAs.

stack.name: Trivy
stack.why: Aqua Security Trivy is Apache-2.0 (no relicensing). Self-hosted scanner (OS pkgs, deps, images, IaC/config drift) run in our own CI/K8s pipeline; operator-side, never shipped to customers -> internal-infra carve-out. Permissive OSS regardless, so product-embeddable even without the exception.

stack.name: Prowler
stack.why: Wiz is a proprietary closed-source managed CNAPP with no self-hostable OSS core (external SaaS we don't operate) -> must be replaced. Prowler (prowler-cloud/prowler) is Apache-2.0 and did NOT relicense (commercial 'Prowler Cloud' SaaS sits on an Apache-2.0 core). Self-hostable CSPM/cloud-posture scanner run operator-side in our pipeline; pairs with Trivy for workload CVE coverage.

stack.name: DefectDojo
stack.why: OWASP DefectDojo is BSD-3-Clause (no relicensing). Self-hosted vulnerability aggregation/dedup hub with SLA-based remediation tracking; operator-side tooling not distributed to customers -> internal-infra carve-out. Permissive OSS anyway.

stack.name: OSV-Scanner
stack.why: Snyk-hosted is a proprietary managed SaaS on the NOT-ACCEPTABLE list -> must be replaced. Google's OSV-Scanner is Apache-2.0 (no relicensing), a self-hostable SCA/dependency scanner run in-pipeline covering the software-side scanning + remediation role (pair with Renovate for auto-fix PRs).

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: Trivy (self-hosted scanning) or Wiz (managed cloud scanning + prioritization) feed findings into DefectDojo, which enforces SLA tracking and remediation workflow; Snyk covers the software/dependency side with auto-fix PRs. Managed alternatives to Wiz in this space include Tenable, Qualys VMDR, and Orca Security. A lighter open-source software-side alternative to Snyk is OSV-Scanner plus Dependabot/Renovate. All four listed tools are current and widely adopted as of 2026; no web search was needed given their established market position.

capabilities.name: System monitoring, alerting & audit log retention
capabilities.description: Continuously monitor system components for anomalies with detection tooling and defined alerting thresholds that generate timely actionable alerts, and retain integrity-protected security logs supporting detection and post-hoc investigation.

stack.name: Prometheus + Alertmanager
stack.why: Scrapes our own system/app metrics and routes threshold-based deduplicated alerts. Apache-2.0 is an acceptable product-embeddable OSS license, so this is kept on its own license merits and does not rely on the internal-infra carve-out; it is operator-side by role but needs no exception.

stack.name: Grafana Loki + Grafana
stack.why: Log aggregation + dashboards/log-alerting over our own stack. Both relicensed to AGPL-3.0 in 2021 (license claim verified, not stale). AGPL network-copyleft is unacceptable for a shipped component, but this is pure operator-side observability that is never distributed to customers, so it qualifies for the internal-infra carve-out (which names Grafana/Loki explicitly).

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: Open SIEM/XDR doing intrusion detection, file-integrity monitoring and security-event correlation on our own infra. GPL-2.0 (verified) is strong copyleft, but it is a pipeline/operator-side security tool run on our own stack and never shipped in the customer product, so the carve-out applies (distribution test: code never reaches the customer).

stack.name: AWS S3 with Object Lock (WORM)
stack.why: Immutable WORM retention tier for our own audit/security logs. Proprietary AWS-managed, which would fail the not-OSS bar for a shipped component, but it is pure operator-side storage of our own logs that is never distributed to or run as the customer product, so the carve-out (ANY license for non-distributed operator infra) applies.

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: Prometheus/Alertmanager for metric-threshold alerting, Loki/Grafana for log analytics and dashboards, Wazuh for security detection and file-integrity monitoring, and S3 Object Lock as the immutable retention tier. Fully-managed alternative if avoiding self-hosting: Datadog (Infrastructure Monitoring + Cloud SIEM + Log Management with retention/archival to immutable storage) or Grafana Cloud, either of which collapses components 1-3 into one SaaS. On GCP/Azure the immutable-retention equivalent is GCS Bucket Lock or Azure Blob immutable storage. All listed tools are actively maintained and current as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Incident response & recovery
capabilities.description: End-to-end incident lifecycle covering triage and severity evaluation, a documented and periodically tested IR plan, containment/eradication/mitigation, breach and stakeholder communication, recovery of affected systems, and post-incident root-cause review with corrective actions.

stack.name: Prometheus Alertmanager
stack.why: Apache-2.0 verified (Prometheus project, no relicensing). Self-hostable alert routing/dedup/silencing/severity paging — operator-side detection/triage, never distributed to customers, so the internal-infra classification is honest. Replaces proprietary managed PagerDuty (no self-hostable OSS core). Apache-2.0 is product-embeddable anyway.

stack.name: Netflix Dispatch
stack.why: Apache-2.0 verified (netflix/dispatch). Self-hosted incident lifecycle orchestration (declare/assign/timeline/RCA) run operator-side, not shipped to customers — internal-infra classification honest. Replaces proprietary managed incident.io (no self-hostable OSS core).

stack.name: Cachet
stack.why: BSD-3-Clause verified — not a relicensing trap (not BSL/SSPL/RSALv2/AGPL). Customer-facing public status page for breach/outage communication, correctly tagged in-product; BSD-3-Clause permits embedding in a proprietary, sold product.

capabilities.stack_notes: Distinct-layer split rather than overlapping platforms: PagerDuty = detection/triage/on-call, incident.io = lifecycle orchestration + comms + post-incident RCA (covers the "documented, periodically tested IR plan" via runbooks and post-mortem workflows), Cachet = external stakeholder communication. Deliberately avoided two now-declining tools: Atlassian Opsgenie (end-of-sale June 2025, full EOL April 2027) and Grafana OnCall OSS (maintenance mode, archived 2026-03-24). Managed alternatives to incident.io in the same tier: Rootly and FireHydrant, both widely adopted in 2025-2026. If a managed status page is acceptable, Atlassian Statuspage is the market default in place of Cachet. Recovery of affected systems (DR/restore) is typically handled by the underlying infra/backup stack rather than these IR tools.

capabilities.name: Change management & secure SDLC
capabilities.description: Formal change process governing authorization, design/impact assessment, testing, independent approval, and implementation, with segregation of duties, version control, separated dev/test/prod environments, baseline configuration and security review, emergency-change and rollback paths, plus general controls over software acquisition, development, and maintenance and their technology dependencies.

stack.name: GitHub (branch protection + CODEOWNERS + required reviews)
stack.why: PR-based change authorization, independent approval and SoD over git version control. Proprietary managed SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core, which would be disqualifying in-product, but this is pure operator-side change-management tooling never distributed to customers, so the internal-infra carve-out applies. Classification is honest: a SOC2 change-management control is inherently operator-side.

stack.name: GitHub Actions with Environments + required reviewers
stack.why: Gated CI/CD with test gates, environment promotion and manual approvals. Proprietary, but internal CI/CD is explicitly named in the carve-out; it runs operator-side and never ships as the customer product, so the exception holds.

stack.name: OpenTofu (Terraform-compatible IaC)
stack.why: Versioned, reviewable infra-as-code with plan/apply gates and drift detection. License claim verified against the Terraform->BSL relicensing trap: the audit correctly cites OpenTofu (Linux Foundation fork) under MPL-2.0, not BSL Terraform. MPL-2.0 is an acceptable file-level-copyleft license and the tooling is operator-side, so no violation.

stack.name: Argo CD (GitOps)
stack.why: Declarative Git-driven deploys with auto/one-click rollback. CNCF graduated project, still Apache-2.0 (no relicensing), an acceptable OSS license, and operator-side delivery tooling not part of the customer runtime.

capabilities.stack_notes: Set chosen for a greenfield 2026 build; all are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. GitHub + Actions cover the formal change process (authorization, independent approval, SoD via CODEOWNERS, testing gates, environment separation). OpenTofu covers baseline configuration-as-code; add a pipeline security scanner such as Trivy or Snyk for the security-review step if a 5th slot is available. Argo CD provides the implementation + rollback path. GitLab (managed or self-hosted) is a viable single-vendor alternative covering the first three roles.

capabilities.name: Privacy notice, consent & lawful collection
capabilities.description: Publish a privacy notice describing collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal of personal information at or before collection, and operate a consent ledger and collection controls that capture affirmative/explicit consent, verify source authority, and keep collection and use within notified purposes.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Fides (github.com/ethyca/fides) is genuinely Apache-2.0 — the OSS privacy-as-code core, distinct from Ethyca's separate commercial product. Serves versioned privacy notices, records consent against a shared data-use ontology, enforces purpose limitation at runtime. Apache-2.0 permits embedding in a sold product. Also absorbs the notice-publishing/consent-ledger role of the dropped proprietary OneTrust.

stack.name: Klaro!
stack.why: Klaro! (github.com/kiprotect/klaro) OSS consent manager is BSD-3-Clause (a separate Klaro Commercial edition exists but is not what is shipped here). Self-hosted web consent manager for explicit affirmative opt-in at the point of collection in the customer-facing app. BSD-3-Clause is fully product-embeddable.

stack.name: Jitsu
stack.why: Replaces proprietary managed Ketch (no self-hostable OSS core). Jitsu (github.com/jitsucom/jitsu) remains MIT-licensed and self-hostable — it did not follow the source-available relicensings that hit RudderStack (Elastic License 2.0) or Snowplow (SLULA), both correctly excluded. Self-hosted OSS data pipeline propagating purpose/consent flags downstream across CDP/ad/AI destinations. MIT is embeddable in a sold product.

capabilities.stack_notes: Fides is the recommended open-source foundation (notice + consent ledger + purpose enforcement, GDPR/CCPA/LGPD built in). OneTrust or Ketch are the mature managed alternatives — Ketch is notable for a server-side ledger that enforces purpose limitation across the data ecosystem. Klaro covers only the front-end capture slice and pairs with a backend ledger. Source authority verification (proving a valid collection source/legal basis) is typically handled by the ledger's consent-record metadata plus your own IAM/identity layer; no single tool fully covers it. Confirmed current 2025-2026: ethyca/fides (github.com/ethyca/fides), ketch.com (Progressive Consent launched 2025).

capabilities.name: Data-subject rights & complaint handling
capabilities.description: Authenticated self-service and back-office workflows that let data subjects access, correct, amend, or delete their personal information and propagate changes to third parties, plus an intake-and-resolution process for privacy inquiries, complaints, and disputes with corrective-action tracking.

stack.name: Ethyca Fides
stack.why: Verified: the Fides privacy-engineering ecosystem is licensed Apache-2.0 (fideslang spec is CC BY 4.0, not shipped as code). OSS DSR engine that data-maps PII and executes access/rectify/erase with third-party propagation; Apache-2.0 permits embedding in a sold product.

stack.name: Flowable
stack.replaced_from: OneTrust Privacy & Data Governance (DSR Automation + Privacy Incident/Complaint Management)
stack.why: Verified: Flowable engine is distributed under Apache-2.0. OneTrust is a proprietary managed SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core; Flowable is a self-hostable Apache-2.0 BPMN/CMMN/DMN engine that runs complaint/dispute intake, resolution SLAs, and corrective-action tracking.

stack.name: Chatwoot
stack.replaced_from: OpenGDPR / self-hosted case management (e.g. Zammad or Camunda) fronting the DSR engine
stack.why: Verified: Chatwoot Community Edition is MIT (only the /enterprise folder is proprietary; ship CE only). Named alternatives fail in-product policy — Zammad is AGPL-3.0 network copyleft; Camunda 8 is source-available under Camunda License 1.0 (since Oct 2024) and Camunda 7 Apache-2.0 hit EOL on 2025-10-14. MIT Chatwoot CE is a self-hostable intake/case tool for authenticated privacy inquiry and complaint handling.

capabilities.stack_notes: Verified current for 2025-2026 via web search. Typical build: Fides or Transcend for the automated DSR access/correct/delete + third-party propagation layer, plus OneTrust (managed) or an open-source case/BPMN tool (Zammad/Camunda) for complaint intake, disputes, and corrective-action tracking. OneTrust and Transcend are the most widely-adopted managed options; Ethyca Fides is the leading open-source DSR-automation engine. Sources: https://www.ethyca.com/guides/dsar-personal-data-tracking-infrastructure , https://www.onetrust.com/products/data-subject-request-dsr-automation/ , https://www.g2.com/compare/onetrust-privacy-automation-vs-transcend

capabilities.name: Privacy breach detection & notification
capabilities.description: Process and tooling to identify, track, and report unauthorized use or disclosure of personal information, notifying affected data subjects and regulators within required timeframes.

stack.name: Wazuh
stack.why: Self-hosted SIEM/XDR run to detect unauthorized access/exfiltration of personal data in our OWN stack (log analysis, file-integrity monitoring, threat rules) — the breach-detection signal. Verified GPL-2.0 (wazuh/wazuh is GPLv2). Strong copyleft, but the binary is never distributed to customers nor run as the product, so the copyleft never reaches the shipped product -> legitimate internal operator-tooling carve-out.

stack.name: DFIR-IRIS
stack.why: Verified LGPL-3.0 (dfir-iris/iris-web). TheHive relicensed at v5 to StrangeBee's proprietary source-available Community license (non-OSI) -> not embeddable in a sold product. DFIR-IRIS is a self-hostable collaborative incident-response platform deployed as a standalone service, so its weak copyleft stays contained (even safer than the dynamic-link case the policy permits) — acceptable in-product. Covers breach case-tracking + defensible audit timeline.

stack.name: Camunda Platform 7
stack.why: OneTrust is a proprietary managed SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core -> violates the OSS goal. Verified Camunda Platform 7 Community Edition is Apache-2.0; correctly pinned to 7 because Camunda 8/Zeebe core is source-available under the Camunda License v1.0. Models the statutory GDPR/CCPA breach-notification workflow with 72h deadline timers and SLA escalation.

stack.name: OpenMetadata
stack.why: Microsoft Purview is a proprietary managed SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core. Verified OpenMetadata is Apache-2.0 (open-metadata/OpenMetadata LICENSE). Data discovery + catalog with automated PII classification, to discover where personal data lives and scope which subjects/record types a breach exposed.

capabilities.stack_notes: Split by function: Wazuh = detection signal, TheHive = investigation/tracking, OneTrust = the statutory notification workflow (the part most specific to this capability), Purview/DSPM = knowing what personal data was exposed to scope notifications. All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Alternatives worth noting: Cyera or BigID in place of Purview for DSPM; Vanta/Drata incident modules as a lighter managed alternative to OneTrust for smaller builds; TheHive can be swapped for a general SOAR if one is already in the stack. A minimal 2-tool build could be Wazuh + OneTrust.

capabilities.name: Personal data quality management
capabilities.description: Mechanisms that keep stored personal information accurate, complete, and relevant to the purposes for which it is used.

stack.name: Great Expectations
stack.why: Declarative expectation suites validate personal records for accuracy/completeness/format at pipeline boundaries with auditable data docs. License verified: GX's OSS core is genuinely Apache-2.0 (the paid GX Cloud is a separate product, not this component); no relicensing. Apache-2.0 permits embedding in a sold product.

stack.name: Soda Core (SodaCL)
stack.why: SQL-based data-quality checks (missing/duplicate/stale rows, freshness, distribution) keep stored personal data correct. License verified: soda-core is Apache-2.0 (Soda Cloud is the separate proprietary SaaS and is not the shipped component); no relicensing. Product-embeddable.

stack.name: dbt Core (tests + snapshots)
stack.why: Generic/built-in tests enforce not-null/unique/accepted-values on PII columns while snapshots track change history. License verified: dbt Core remains Apache-2.0. Scoping is accurate and material — dbt Cloud is proprietary and the 2025 dbt Fusion engine ships under Elastic License 2.0 (non-acceptable source-available), but neither is referenced here; the shipped Core engine is Apache-2.0.

stack.name: Elementary Data
stack.why: Self-hostable, dbt-native data observability (automated anomaly/freshness/volume monitoring + lineage) catching personal-data quality drift at scale. License verified: the elementary dbt package and edr CLI are Apache-2.0 and self-hostable (Elementary Cloud is the separate proprietary SaaS). Correctly replaces Monte Carlo, which is genuinely proprietary managed-SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026. Open-source options (Great Expectations, Soda Core, dbt) cover in-pipeline validation and are typically layered together; Monte Carlo (or alternatives like Ataccama ONE / Collibra DQ for MDM-heavy needs) adds managed observability. A pragmatic new build usually pairs dbt tests + Soda/Great Expectations for enforcement, adding a managed observability layer only when data estate grows.

capabilities.name: Processing integrity: validation, pipeline & output verification
capabilities.description: Documented processing specifications with intake controls validating inputs and authorizing sources, exactly-once complete/accurate/timely pipeline execution with dead-letter and reconciliation, and pre-release output verification, authorized delivery, and durable protected storage of inputs and outputs.

stack.name: Temporal
stack.why: Durable execution engine providing exactly-once, idempotent pipeline steps with retries/timeouts/dead-letter/compensation; the self-hostable Temporal server (temporalio/temporal) is MIT-licensed and embeddable in a proprietary product. Temporal Cloud is a separate proprietary SaaS but is not what is embedded.

stack.name: Great Expectations
stack.why: Declarative data-contract validations for intake controls and pre-release output verification with durable per-run evidence; the GX core library is Apache-2.0 and permits embedding in a sold product (GX Cloud is a distinct proprietary SaaS, not the embedded library).

stack.name: Apache Kafka with Apicurio Registry
stack.why: Kafka core is Apache-2.0, but Confluent Schema Registry is source-available (Confluent Community License, non-OSI) and not embeddable; Apicurio Registry (Apache-2.0) is a drop-in OSS schema registry preserving authorized/schema-validated intact intake plus DLQ/offsets for reconciliation.

stack.name: SeaweedFS (S3 Object Lock / WORM)
stack.why: Amazon S3 is a proprietary managed service with no self-hostable OSS core; SeaweedFS (Apache-2.0) is a self-hostable S3-compatible store supporting Object Lock/WORM retention and versioning for tamper-evident storage of inputs/outputs (MinIO correctly avoided as it relicensed to AGPL-3.0 in 2021, unacceptable in-product).

capabilities.stack_notes: Pattern: Kafka+Schema Registry for authorized/validated intake and dead-letter, Temporal for exactly-once durable pipeline execution with retries/compensation, Great Expectations (or Soda) for intake and pre-release output verification, S3 Object Lock for WORM storage of inputs/outputs. dbt tests are a strong alternative to GX for batch/warehouse pipelines. GCP/Azure equivalents for WORM: GCS Bucket Lock, Azure Blob immutable storage. All confirmed current and widely adopted as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: RBAC, Least Privilege & Identity Lifecycle
capabilities.description: Central identity provider with unique per-principal identities, a documented access-control policy, role-based least-privilege authorization, secure credential/secret handling, a joiner-mover-leaver provisioning flow with periodic recertification, elevated controls for privileged/break-glass accounts, and automatic access revocation on role change or termination.

stack.name: Keycloak
stack.why: Self-hostable OIDC/SAML IdP (CNCF project) providing per-principal identities and realm/role-based least-privilege RBAC. Apache-2.0 confirmed as current license (no relicensing); embeds freely in a proprietary sold product. Dropping the managed Entra ID/Okta option removes a proprietary managed-SaaS duplicate of this same IdP role.

stack.name: OpenBao
stack.replaced_from: HashiCorp Vault (self-hosted or HCP Vault managed)
stack.why: HashiCorp Vault relicensed to BUSL-1.1 (source-available, not embeddable in a proprietary product). OpenBao is the Linux Foundation MPL-2.0 fork of the last pre-BSL Vault codebase, delivering the same short-lived dynamic secrets, automatic rotation and lease-based least-privilege credential access. MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft) is acceptable for in-product embedding.

stack.name: Pomerium
stack.why: Teleport's OSS core repo relicensed from Apache-2.0 to AGPL-3.0 (Dec 2023), and from Teleport 16 (June 2024) its distributed binaries carry a source-available commercial license restricting company use — non-acceptable for a shipped product on both counts. Pomerium's open-source core is Apache-2.0 (verified), an identity-aware access proxy giving per-request IdP-based authorization for privileged/break-glass access, audit logging, and access revocation on IdP role change or termination.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. Pick one primary IdP (managed Entra ID/Okta for fastest governance/recertification, or Keycloak if self-hosting is required) rather than both. Entra ID Governance / Okta Identity Governance cover the access-control policy, JML provisioning, recertification and automatic deprovisioning on termination; Vault covers secret handling; Teleport covers privileged/break-glass elevation and session audit. SCIM provisioning from the IdP to downstream apps ties revocation-on-role-change together end to end.

capabilities.name: Data Classification, Asset Inventory & Secure Data Lifecycle
capabilities.description: An owned asset/information inventory with a sensitivity classification and labelling scheme, acceptable-use and handling rules, encrypted and controlled transfer channels, asset return on offboarding, and verified data sanitization or secure destruction before equipment reuse, disposal, or off-site maintenance.

stack.name: Snipe-IT
stack.why: IT hardware/asset inventory with per-asset ownership, sensitivity custom fields, and check-in/check-out enforcing asset return on offboarding. AGPL-3.0 confirmed, but pure operator-side tooling for our own equipment, never distributed to customers, so the network copyleft never reaches the product (carve-out).

stack.name: Microsoft Presidio
stack.why: PII/sensitive-data detection, classification and de-identification/anonymization for controlled transfer. MIT confirmed; self-hostable and embeddable in a sold product. Replaces proprietary managed-SaaS Purview (no self-hostable OSS core).

stack.name: OpenMetadata
stack.why: Data-asset catalog that auto-classifies and tags datasets (PII/sensitivity) across their lifecycle — the inventory + labelling layer for structured data. Apache-2.0 confirmed against the upstream LICENSE; no paywalled core or source-available relicensing. Permits embedding in a proprietary product.

stack.name: nwipe
stack.why: Certified drive erasure (DoD 5220.22-M / NIST 800-88 style) with verifiable erase logs before equipment reuse/disposal. GPL-2.0 confirmed. Acceptable because it runs operator-side as a standalone tool on our own decommissioned drives, never distributed to customers (carve-out). Replaces proprietary Blancco with a self-hostable OSS eraser.

capabilities.stack_notes: Open-source alternative for verified sanitization: nwipe/ShredOS (drive wiping) though it lacks Blancco's audit-grade certificates. Encrypted/controlled transfer channels are largely covered by the Purview DLP layer plus standard TLS/managed file-transfer; a dedicated MFT (e.g. GoAnywhere) can be added if regulated bulk transfers are in scope. All four confirmed current and actively maintained as of 2025-2026.

capabilities.name: Cryptography: Encryption in Transit, At Rest & Key Management
capabilities.description: A documented cryptography policy enforcing strong current algorithms and adequate key lengths, TLS protection for all sensitive/personal data in transit (including service-to-service), encryption at rest for disks, databases and backups, and full-lifecycle management of keys, certificates and secrets (generation, storage, rotation, revocation, destruction) with tightly restricted access.

stack.name: OpenBao
stack.why: Central engine for full key/secret lifecycle (generation, storage, rotation, revocation, destruction), built-in PKI CA, dynamic DB creds and scoped access policies. HashiCorp Vault relicensed to BSL 1.1 (source-available, non-OSI) in 2023, unacceptable for an in-product runtime. Verified swap to OpenBao, the Linux Foundation fork forked pre-relicense, which retains MPL-2.0 (file-level copyleft, on the acceptable list) and permits embedding in a proprietary product.

stack.name: SoftHSM2 (PKCS#11) as key root of trust
stack.replaced_from: Cloud KMS / HSM (AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, or Azure Key Vault Managed HSM)
stack.why: Provides the self-hostable cryptographic root of trust for envelope encryption of disks/DBs/backups that OpenBao seals against. AWS/GCP/Azure KMS are proprietary managed SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core, so correctly rejected. SoftHSM2 (OpenDNSSEC project) is BSD-2-Clause, verified current, embeddable, and can front a real PKCS#11 HSM in production.

stack.name: cert-manager + Let's Encrypt/ACME
stack.why: Automates TLS certificate issuance, renewal and revocation across the platform so all sensitive/personal data in transit is protected. cert-manager is Apache-2.0 (CNCF graduated project), verified current, fully embeddable in a proprietary product. ACME is an open protocol and Let's Encrypt is an external CA service, not a shipped component.

stack.name: Istio (or Linkerd) service mesh
stack.why: Transparently enforces mutual-TLS with modern ciphers and short-lived rotating certs on every service-to-service call, closing the internal-traffic gap edge TLS leaves open. Istio is Apache-2.0 (CNCF graduated). stack.why: Self-hostable PII discovery/tagging/de-identification embedded in the product's data pipelines and LLM guardrails (privacy-by-design). License verified: Microsoft ships Presidio under MIT, which permits embedding in a sold proprietary product. Role in-product is honest.

stack.name: Klaro
stack.why: Transcend is a proprietary managed SaaS with no self-hostable OSS core and runs on the customer-facing consent/retention data flow, violating policy. Klaro (kiprotect community edition) is verified BSD-3-Clause — a permissive acceptable license — covering the consent-capture/enforcement leg self-hosted.

stack.name: CISO Assistant
stack.why: Vanta is a proprietary managed GRC SaaS with no self-hostable core (not carve-out eligible). CISO Assistant (intuitem) is verified AGPL-3.0 and maintains the legal/regulatory obligations register mapped to controls across 30+ frameworks incl. ISO 27001. AGPL is acceptable here because a GRC register is genuinely operator-side infra, never distributed to customers or run as the product — the network copyleft never reaches customers.

stack.name: OSS Review Toolkit (ORT)
stack.why: Runs in our CI pipeline to scan our own dependencies for license/IP obligations and emit SPDX/CycloneDX SBOMs — operator-side tooling not shipped to customers. License verified Apache-2.0, which is a permissive acceptable license, so it is kept on license merit; it does not need the internal-infra exception.

capabilities.stack_notes: Chosen to cover the three distinct sub-domains of this capability: (1) PII-aware data handling = Presidio; (2) consent + retention enforcement = Transcend; (3) obligations-register-mapped-to-controls = Vanta; (4) IP/software-licensing = ORT. All four verified current as of 2026 via web search. Substitution notes: OneTrust is the higher-mindshare (17.3% DPMS) but heavier alternative to Transcend and can also serve as the obligations register if you prefer one privacy suite over Vanta; Drata is an equivalent managed GRC alternative to Vanta; FOSSA/Black Duck are managed alternatives to ORT with stronger license-edge-case databases. For a greenfield 2026 build, Presidio + ORT (open-source, embed-in-pipeline) plus one managed privacy platform (Transcend) and one managed GRC backbone (Vanta) balances engineering control against auditable, framework-mapped evidence.

capabilities.stack_notes: All four verified current for 2025-2026. Vanta and KnowBe4 both have active 2026 product releases (Vanta multi-source training assignment; KnowBe4 AIDA phishing orchestration). Division of labor: Vanta = policy/acknowledgment/training-tracking/offboarding governance layer; KnowBe4 = actual awareness-training content + phishing + disciplinary risk signal; Checkr = pre-employment screening; BookStack = the SOP/operating-procedure documentation itself. Alternatives worth noting: Drata or Secureframe substitute for Vanta; Hoxhunt or Curricula substitute for KnowBe4; Certn substitutes for Checkr; GitBook, Notion, or Confluence substitute for BookStack if a managed docs tool is preferred over self-hosting. Counterparty NDA e-signing (vs. internal policy acknowledgment, which Vanta covers) would need a signature tool like DocuSign if that is in scope.

capabilities.name: ICT Continuity & Disaster Recovery
capabilities.description: Backup, redundancy and failover capabilities with defined RTO/RPO targets, plus documented and regularly tested restore procedures so information and systems can be recovered to meet business-continuity objectives.

stack.name: Bacula
stack.why: AWS Backup only performs its job (policy-driven backup jobs, retention, restore tests) on paid usage — it bills per GB of backup storage, per restore, and for cross-region/cross-account copies, with no free tier that covers the actual backup function. The internal function (centralized, policy-scheduled backup and restore verification of our own AWS estate) is covered by Bacula, a mature free OSS backup solution that is self-hostable at no cost, supports schedule/retention policies, catalog-driven centralized management, and restore testing against EC2/EBS/RDS-exported data and S3. License AGPL-3.0.

stack.name: DRBD (with Pacemaker/Corosync for automated failover)
stack.why: AWS DRS only offers a limited free tier (~2160 hours / 90 days per source server); the stated use is continuous, indefinite block-level replication plus standing failover readiness, which runs on paid per-server hourly charges and standing staging EBS/EC2 costs beyond that window — so the tool does its actual job only on a paid basis. It is a managed software service, not the cloud substrate/attestation/legal/physical category, so the inherent exception does not apply. DRBD (GPL-2.0) provides the same continuous block-level replication and, combined with Pacemaker/Corosync, delivers automated failover at minutes-scale RTO — a free, self-hostable OSS equivalent covering the same ISO 27001 ICT continuity and disaster-recovery function.

stack.name: Velero
stack.why: CNCF Kubernetes backup + cross-cluster restore of our OWN cluster state and PVs; operator-side DR infra. License verified: still Apache-2.0 in 2026 (not on any relicensing watchlist), which is an ACCEPTABLE product-embeddable OSS license outright, so it is kept on license merit and does NOT require the internal-tooling carve-out.

stack.name: pgBackRest
stack.why: PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery with parallel/incremental encrypted backups of our OWN database to hit tight RPO. License verified: still MIT, an ACCEPTABLE permissive OSS license, so this operator-side backup engine is kept on license merit and does NOT need the carve-out. (Only the backup tool is in scope here, not an in-product datastore, so the internal-infra classification is honest.)

capabilities.stack_notes: Layered coverage: DRS for VM/server-level failover, Velero for Kubernetes, pgBackRest for database PITR, AWS Backup as the governing backup/restore-test policy plane. All are widely adopted and current as of 2025-2026. Cloud-agnostic swaps if not on AWS: Azure Site Recovery / Google Backup and DR for the managed pieces; restic or Kopia as an open-source general-purpose backup engine. Whichever stack is chosen, the compliance requirement demands scheduled restore drills and documented RTO/RPO per system, not just backup configuration.
